thebarapp.name: TheBarApp
thebarapp.phase: Testing the demo at Das Wohnzimmer

audit.summary: TheBarApp is the all-in-one system built for Das Wohnzimmer in Wiesbaden — staff scheduling, stock, recipes, menus, the till, and an in-app assistant. This stretch added a daily cash register, a full digital-menu module (with a public page you can build from a photo or even your voice), privacy-safe staff avatars, and closed a serious cross-venue privacy gap. It's feature-complete and healthy; right now it's being tried out as a demo at Das Wohnzimmer — going live there for real is the next milestone.

chapters.title: One system to run a venue
chapters.what: TheBarApp handles the whole operation of a bar or restaurant in one place — staff scheduling, stock, recipes, menus, the daily till, and an assistant that answers questions and takes action. The first venue is Das Wohnzimmer in Wiesbaden, where it's currently being tested as a demo.
chapters.why: Venues juggle a dozen tools; one system that does it all is the whole pitch.

chapters.title: The daily basics, built
chapters.what: Built and being demo-tested for Das Wohnzimmer: smart staff scheduling, stock and recipe management, scanning a paper menu into the app, and a morning briefing with real forecast numbers.
chapters.why: These are the things a venue touches every single day — they had to work first.

chapters.title: Closed a privacy gap between venues
chapters.what: Found and fixed a serious issue where one venue could see another's reservations, regulars and assistant data. Fixed it, cleaned up the affected records, deployed to the live server, and proved each venue now only sees its own.
chapters.why: Keeping each venue's data separate is non-negotiable — trust is the product.

chapters.title: The assistant learned to act, not just chat
chapters.what: The in-app assistant (Wozi) can now carry out real actions from a message — like reporting someone sick or offering a shift — and always asks you to confirm first so nothing happens by accident.
chapters.why: It turns a chatbot into a genuine helper that saves the manager time.

chapters.title: A daily cash register — 'the bank'
chapters.what: Built a daily till module: count the drawer at close, see the day's real profit. It was built in a safe sandbox first so it could never touch live data by accident, then shipped to the live server switched off — ready to turn on for Das Wohnzimmer whenever you choose.
chapters.why: Gives the venue a clean, honest end-of-day money picture — built carefully because money is sensitive.

chapters.title: Made the till match real life
chapters.what: Added 'other costs' (things paid out of the till or someone's own pocket) and polished the screens after a live demo. A test day came out to a clean profit of 1.541,80 €.
chapters.why: The till has to mirror how money actually moves day to day, not a tidy theory.

chapters.title: A full digital-menu module
chapters.what: Venues can now build and edit their own menu in the dashboard, and it gets a clean public web page with its own link and a QR code — three polished design themes, allergen info, and proper German prices.
chapters.why: A modern, shareable menu built right into the platform — no separate tool needed.

chapters.title: A menu from a photo, a file, or your voice
chapters.what: Added a way to fill a menu automatically — upload a photo or file of an existing menu, paste a link, or just speak it — and it drafts the items for you to review. For now this runs on test venues only, while we clear the data-protection steps before real venues use it.
chapters.why: Turns a printed menu into a digital one in minutes instead of typing every dish.

chapters.title: Privacy-safe staff avatars
chapters.what: Designed simple drawn avatars for staff — not photos and not AI faces — so the schedule and feed feel personal without ever storing anyone's picture. Built and waiting on a final check on a real phone.
chapters.why: Warmth and personality without the privacy cost or expense of real photos.

chapters.title: The honest blocker: Apple, the tax advisor, a phone check
chapters.what: The app is feature-complete and healthy. The remaining steps to the public beta are outside coding: Apple's review of the latest build, the tax advisor's confirmed VAT rates (to switch the till from gross to net), and two quick checks on a real phone.
chapters.why: Naming the real waits keeps expectations honest — the code is ready; people and process are the gate.

bloghead.name: Bloghead
bloghead.phase: In internal TestFlight — payments in test mode

audit.summary: Bloghead started as a website, then moved onto the iPhone. Over the last weeks it crossed the line from 'looks finished' to 'actually works' — a booking now runs all the way through with a real invoice, the app runs on a real phone with real photos and real logins, and it backs itself up every night. The one big piece left before it's a real business is taking payments, which is being wired up now.

chapters.title: The website came first
chapters.what: The web version was built and polished — artist profiles, search and booking — loading fast with top marks for speed, search-friendliness and accessibility.
chapters.why: Prove the idea works and have something real on the web before committing to a full phone app.

chapters.title: Moving onto the iPhone
chapters.what: The artist search, booking-request and profile screens were rebuilt natively for iPhone, all working against the live server.
chapters.why: The phone is where artists, organizers and fans actually are — a website alone wasn't going to be enough.

chapters.title: A booking finally completes, start to finish
chapters.what: For the first time ever, a booking went all the way through — request, to confirmed, to done — and the invoice was created automatically. The thing that had blocked this for a long time turned out to be a hidden fault deep in the database; once found it was fixed and protected with a test so it can't quietly come back.
chapters.why: A marketplace that can't finish a booking isn't a business. This unlocked the whole point of the app.

chapters.title: Real photos instead of placeholders
chapters.what: Swapped stock placeholder images for 60 real, made-for-us pictures of artists and venues.
chapters.why: First impressions matter — and it also removed a legal risk that came with using people's photos without permission.

chapters.title: In your hand for the first time
chapters.what: The app was installed and opened on a real iPhone, connected to the live server — animated intro, login and real artist faces all working.
chapters.why: You only truly know something works when it's running on a real phone, not just on the computer.

chapters.title: Letting people sign in easily
chapters.what: Sign in with Google and with Apple were both proven working on the live server — Apple for the very first time.
chapters.why: Nobody wants to invent yet another password. Easy sign-in is the difference between someone joining and giving up.

chapters.title: Something alive when you open it
chapters.what: Filled the discovery feed with 12 real upcoming events across Wiesbaden, Mainz and Frankfurt, sorted by how close they are.
chapters.why: An empty app feels dead. A full, local feed makes it feel alive from the very first second.

chapters.title: Never losing anything
chapters.what: Set up automatic nightly backups plus a watchdog that restarts the app if it ever freezes, with an alert to the phone.
chapters.why: The moment real people put real information in, losing it is simply not an option.

chapters.title: Getting artists paid
chapters.what: Wiring up the payment system (Stripe) so artists can actually be paid, with our small fee taken automatically. Test keys are in hand; it isn't switched on yet.
chapters.why: This is the last big piece before Bloghead is a real, working business — so it's the current focus.

dehgo.name: Dehgo
dehgo.phase: Built — waiting on legal & domain to launch

audit.summary: DOGA (working name for TBD) connects hospitality venues with local part-time workers (Aushilfen) across the Rhein-Main area. The core shift loop now works end to end — proven on a real phone and the venue dashboard — and the safety issues from review are closed, the server is prepared, and all the work is safely backed up. The honest blocker to launching for real isn't the code: it's legal sign-off, signed data-handling agreements, and a domain with a security certificate.

chapters.title: A connector, not a staffing agency
chapters.what: DOGA introduces venues to nearby part-time workers: a venue posts a shift, workers apply, the venue picks who it wants, and a chat opens so they sort the details.
chapters.why: Staying a connector — where the venue alone decides and we never touch wages — is what keeps the product on the right side of German staffing law.

chapters.title: Building both sides
chapters.what: Built the worker iPhone app and the venue web dashboard: posting jobs, reviewing applicants, profiles, chat, and safety tools like report and block.
chapters.why: It's a two-sided marketplace — it only works if both the venue side and the worker side do.

chapters.title: A clear plan for the whole product
chapters.what: Put the full vision through an expert review and locked a build order — first a lawful, polished shift-loop, then the bigger features later. Nothing was cut, just sequenced, with the legal lines drawn up front.
chapters.why: So we build the right things in the right order without tripping over the law later.

chapters.title: The gig loop works end to end
chapters.what: Proved the heart of the product — find a shift, apply, get accepted, do the job — working all the way through on both the phone and the venue dashboard, with a realistic test set (50 workers, 10 venues).
chapters.why: A marketplace that can't complete its core loop isn't a product yet. Now it can.

chapters.title: Safety and correctness pass
chapters.what: Closed five issues from review — including making sure a worker can never reach venue-only screens and a shift can't be accidentally filled twice — and fixed photo uploads and chat reliability.
chapters.why: Trust and correctness have to be right before real people rely on it.

chapters.title: Right distances everywhere
chapters.what: The app had assumed everyone was in Frankfurt, so distances were wrong for workers elsewhere; it now uses each worker's real city.
chapters.why: Distance is the whole point of shift work — it has to be correct beyond a single city.

chapters.title: On a real phone — and the bugs it found
chapters.what: Installed it on a real iPhone for the first time. Real-device testing surfaced three issues (the keyboard hiding the chat 'send', a silent application confirmation, un-tappable rows); all three are fixed, with one keyboard check left.
chapters.why: Simulators don't catch everything — a real phone does.

chapters.title: Ready to deploy, safely stored
chapters.what: Prepared everything to run on our server and backed all the work up online so nothing lives on a single computer. The server is configured but not switched on yet.
chapters.why: No risk of losing work, and a clean switch-on once the launch gates clear.

chapters.title: Held back the messaging feature on purpose
chapters.what: Planned a richer messaging feature (templates, attachments) but deliberately parked it — it would add an outside AI service and make the legal approval bigger, right when legal is already the #1 thing holding up launch.
chapters.why: Don't enlarge the legal pile right before launch; revisit it later as a deliberate choice.

chapters.title: The honest blocker: the lawyer, not the code
chapters.what: Launching for real is waiting on things outside engineering — written legal sign-off, signed data-handling agreements with our service providers, and a website address with a security certificate. The server is ready to switch on the moment those clear.
chapters.why: A ready server doesn't make a launch lawful — being honest about the real gate keeps expectations right.

no1restaurant.name: No.1 Restaurant
no1restaurant.phase: Live — going for the signed contract

log.title: Morning briefing shows real numbers
log.detail: The morning briefing inside the app now shows actual forecast numbers — like '€1,850 expected tonight' — instead of placeholder text. It's pulling live data.

log.title: Website speed score improved
log.detail: Ran a performance check after some loading tweaks. Speed score went from 93 to 95 out of 100. Search engine and accessibility scores are still perfect 100s.

log.title: Schedule preview screen built
log.detail: New screen where you can see and edit the auto-generated staff schedule before approving it. The screen is ready — connecting it to the scheduling engine is next.

log.title: Looked into live typing indicators
log.detail: Checked what it would take to add 'typing...' indicators and online status in the chat. It's doable (about 4–6 hours) but parked for now — not blocking anything.

log.title: Fixed crate counting mistake
log.detail: A crate (Kiste) was being recorded as 1 item instead of 24 bottles. Stock numbers now add up correctly. Re-running the full inventory check once missing supplier invoices are in.

log.title: Artist search + booking screens built
log.detail: The artist search and booking request screens are now built in the iPhone app. They work against the live backend. Login and payment come next.

log.title: This dashboard went live
log.detail: The shared progress page you're reading right now was set up and connected. Updates show here automatically whenever a step is finished.

log.title: Menu scan works in the background
log.detail: Uploading a menu photo no longer freezes the app. It now processes in the background — you can keep using the app while it works, and it notifies you when it's done.

log.title: Allergen labels are now accurate
log.detail: Allergen warnings on scanned menu items are now calculated from the actual saved recipe ingredients, not guessed from the printed menu text. Much more reliable — if a recipe has egg, it will correctly say 'Contains: Egg'.

log.title: App speaks proper German now
log.detail: Auto-generated recipes now use correct German terms throughout — glasses (Rocks-Glas), preparation methods (Shaken), and units (Stück) instead of English placeholders.

log.title: Menu scan photos upload reliably
log.detail: Large photos no longer crash during upload. The review screen is also cleaner — long drink names don't overflow, and suggested ingredients show in a tidy collapsed list.

log.title: 8 cocktail recipes filled in properly
log.detail: Eight classics in Das Wohnzimmer's menu — Caipirinha, Daiquiri, Mojito, Margarita, Gin Basil Smash, Midori Sour, Vodka Sour, Whiskey Sour — were upgraded from skeleton entries to full recipes with real ingredients. Three duplicate/empty entries were also cleaned out.

log.title: Recognised drinks show correct allergens
log.detail: When the app recognises a drink from a menu scan, it now shows allergens from the actual saved recipe — not from whatever text was printed on the menu. Verified: Vodka Sour and Whiskey Sour correctly flag 'Egg' allergen on the live server.

log.title: App builds cleanly — one-command setup
log.detail: Fixed the build environment from scratch: updated the underlying tools to the latest versions and wrote a single-command local setup so any new machine can be fully running in minutes. First real foundation for everything that follows.

log.title: Venue dashboard, job posting + settings done
log.detail: Three major screens finished for venue owners: a live dashboard showing stats and recent jobs, a step-by-step job posting wizard (with legal minimum-wage enforcement — €12.81/h as required by German law), and a venue settings page. All 6 key flows tested end to end and passing.

log.title: Applicant review, chat + notifications wired
log.detail: Venue owners can now see a ranked list of applicants for each job, view their profiles, accept or reject them, and chat with them. Workers automatically get a push notification the moment they're accepted or rejected. Phase 4 is fully complete.

log.title: Project moved to new MacBook — all working
log.detail: Migrated the entire development setup from the old Mac mini to the new MacBook Pro. Database, app build, admin tools — all verified. The project was also pushed to GitHub for the first time (it had only ever existed locally until this point).

log.title: Privacy + safety features planned and started
log.detail: Mapped out all the GDPR data-protection and content-moderation features the app needs before it can go public. Wrote a formal legal briefing with 9 questions for a lawyer — two of them (around data brokering and automated decisions) are hard blockers for launch. Also built the foundation: background job scheduler and email sending system.

log.title: Report + block system built
log.detail: Users can now report each other (7 predefined reasons in German, max 10 per day) and block each other. Blocking hides the other person from your job feed in both directions and freezes the chat. Thoroughly tested — 95%+ test coverage on these features.

log.title: Fixed: app couldn't actually be logged into
log.detail: Discovered that email/password login had never been connected — only Apple Sign-In existed. The whole signup and login flow is now properly wired. Fixing this revealed two crashes that had been hiding the entire time: the job feed was silently failing on every load, and all timestamps were being rejected app-wide. Both fixed.

log.title: iOS tests restored + critical chat bug fixed
log.detail: An automated hardening pass (36 minutes of agent time): the iOS test suite was brought back to life — 27 tests now run and pass (the suite had never compiled before). Fixed a bug where workers couldn't access the chat at all. Also corrected several mismatches between what the server sends and what the app expects.

log.title: App screens rebuilt to match the designs
log.detail: None of the screens had ever been compared against the actual design mockups — they had the right colours and fonts but the wrong layouts. Fixed the comparison process, then rebuilt 6 screens to exactly match: worker job feed, job detail, job posting form, applicant list, venue onboarding, and the venue detail section. Design-accurate for the first time.

log.title: App rebuilt cleanly on a real iPhone
log.detail: Tracked down the existing Bloghead app, rebuilt it from scratch, and got it running on a real iPhone 13 Pro Max with zero errors and zero warnings. Several small problems that had crept in were fixed along the way — the cleanest possible starting point before the big sprint.

log.title: Full audit: 10 real problems found
log.detail: Rather than assume the app was in good shape, we ran a top-to-bottom inspection of every feature. Found ten significant gaps — including a booking fee set to the wrong percentage and a privacy policy promising a feature that didn't actually exist. Every decision that followed was based on facts, not guesswork. Catching this early saved enormous time and protected the business.

log.title: Booking fee fixed; false privacy claim removed
log.detail: Two urgent corrections: the platform fee was wrong (10% instead of the intended 8%) — every booking would have overcharged artists. The privacy policy also described an AI feature we hadn't built, which is a real legal risk under German consumer law. Both fixed with small but very high-consequence changes.

log.title: Animated new-user welcome journey built
log.detail: Brand-new first-time experience: a polished logo introduction, a three-page tour explaining what Bloghead does (Discover → Book → Connect), a role-selection screen, and a clear notification explanation before asking permission. Fixed a hidden bug where choosing 'I'm an artist' on the welcome screen was being silently thrown away — the choice now carries through properly.

log.title: Privacy consent + report/block tools added
log.detail: During sign-up, people now clearly agree to terms and privacy (required) and can separately choose marketing emails and anonymous statistics (optional) — proper DSGVO consent done right. Also built report and block tools: anyone can report inappropriate content or block a user, who then disappears from their view across the entire app. Required for Apple App Store approval.

log.title: Organizer and Crew roles built end to end
log.detail: Expanded who can use Bloghead. Organizers (event planners) existed on the welcome screen but were secretly treated as regular fans — fixed properly end to end. Crew (sound engineers, lighting techs, stage crew, security) is a brand-new role with its own profile showing specializations, equipment, and hourly rates. Real events need more than just an artist and a venue.

log.title: Old platform leftovers fully cleared out
log.detail: The app was originally built on a different platform that we had since moved away from. Over 1,000 leftover files were still scattered through the code — confusing and potentially a red flag during Apple's review. All of it removed cleanly: old files, old config, outdated documentation rewritten to reflect reality. Like clearing the workshop before building the fine furniture.

log.title: Artist availability + tech rider now working
log.detail: Two features had screens in the app but weren't connected to anything — they silently showed nothing. Fixed both: artists can now block out dates they're unavailable, and specify their sound, lighting, and stage requirements. Rather than guess what a weekly schedule feature should look like, we chose to ask real artists first — build what people actually need.

log.title: Full digital contract system built
log.detail: Complete contract engine for bookings: generates a proper, legally structured contract in German, English, or French; both sides digitally sign; the contract locks permanently once signed and can never be secretly altered — a strict legal requirement. Keeps a tamper-proof history of every action. Cancellation rules come in presets (Relaxed, Standard, Strict, Festival, Custom). Reviewed by a German contract-law specialist before a line of code was written.

log.title: Invoice + credit note engine built
log.detail: Automatic, legally compliant invoicing: when an event is completed, the system creates a proper invoice, calculates the correct German VAT (small-business exemption, 7% cultural rate, or 19% standard — whichever applies), assigns a gap-free invoice number, generates a PDF, and emails it automatically. Cancelled bookings trigger a matching credit note. All invoices are locked and tamper-proof. German tax law is unforgiving, and this handles it properly so everyone stays compliant without thinking about it.

log.title: Full mobile experience for all new features
log.detail: Every new system brought to life on the actual phone: Crew sign-up and profiles, an Events area for organizers and venues, viewing and signing contracts, a full Accounting area (Buchhaltung) where users see all their invoices and can view or download the PDFs, and smart deep links so tapping a notification opens exactly the right screen. Each role only sees what's relevant to them — fans get a simple app, professionals get the full toolkit.

log.title: Sign contracts without installing the app
log.detail: The most innovative piece of the sprint. Technical crew (sound, lighting) often work informally and won't install a new app just to sign one contract. Solution: an organizer invites a crew member by email, who clicks a secure link and signs the contract directly in their web browser — no app, no account needed. Legally valid under German law with a full audit trail. They only create an account later, when there's money to be paid — the moment it actually benefits them.

log.title: Publishing pipeline fixed and automated
log.detail: Discovered during the audit that a batch of completed work had been built but never actually published to the live server — features we thought were live, weren't. Traced the cause, published everything correctly, and made the process automatic going forward so this can't happen again. Also strengthened how the database updates itself safely.

log.title: Users can request or fully delete their data
log.detail: Anyone using the app can now request a complete copy of their personal data, or delete their account entirely — with a 30-day window to change their mind before anything is gone for good. Deletion genuinely removes their information everywhere it lives across the system. This is a legal requirement under EU data-protection law (DSGVO) and was tested rigorously to make sure one person's deletion never accidentally touches anyone else's data.

log.title: Report, block + auto-moderation system built
log.detail: Three layers of protection now in place: users can report or block each other; the system automatically flags suspicious chat messages (attempts to move deals off-platform, spam, scams) for review; and admins can ban bad actors — instantly removing their job posts, cancelling pending matches, and locking them out. A two-sided marketplace lives or dies on trust, and this keeps the platform clean.

log.title: Abuse limits + SMS cost protection added
log.detail: Added limits that stop people from hammering the system: protection against password-guessing attacks, mass fake-account creation, and abuse of the text-message verification system — which costs real money per message sent. Without these, a single bad actor could run up a real bill or compromise accounts.

log.title: Error monitoring + daily backups wired up
log.detail: The app now automatically reports errors the moment they happen, tracks key activity (sign-ups, jobs posted, matches made), and backs itself up every day — with a tested recovery process so data can be restored if something ever goes wrong. Once live, we'll see problems immediately instead of hearing about them from frustrated users, and a server failure becomes an inconvenience, not a catastrophe.

log.title: App visuals confirmed matching the design
log.detail: Ran a full side-by-side check of every screen against the original design — this time with real data loaded, not placeholder content. The app now looks exactly like the professional product we designed, not a rough prototype. First impressions are everything in a consumer app; venues and workers judge credibility in seconds.

log.title: Mitarbeiter onboarding T1
log.detail: Employee model +7 DATEV fields, StaffService actor stubs (6 endpoints), 4-tier chooser (Import/Scannen/Einladen stubs + Manuell fully built with Lohndaten amber section + IBAN eye-reveal)

log.title: First hands-on test on a real iPhone
log.detail: Installed Bloghead on a real iPhone and used it exactly the way a customer would — for the first time. Automated checks can only do so much; real-world use immediately surfaced problems that no test could catch. This is the phase where a product proves itself in real life, not just on paper.

log.title: Booking request now works end to end
log.detail: Sending a booking request was failing with an error on a real device — and booking is the entire heart of the platform. Fixed it properly, then verified the full journey on the phone: discover an artist → send a booking → artist accepts → contract created automatically. The most important action in the app now works as it should.

log.title: Logout trap, blank venues + welcome flow fixed
log.detail: Three real-world bugs found and fixed on the actual phone: logging out left users trapped with no way forward (now cleanly returns to the start); tapping any venue opened a blank screen (now loads properly); new users could pick their role but then hit a dead end — the welcome journey now leads all the way through to sign-up and the right setup screen for each role.

log.title: All 5 account types can now fully sign up
log.detail: Fan, Artist, Organizer, Venue, and Crew can each register and reach their own correct setup screen. Two of them — Crew and Organizer — couldn't complete sign-up before. Both fixed. Every type of person Bloghead is built for can now actually get in the door.

log.title: Hidden feature connected; full reachability check done
log.detail: The Technical Rider tool — where artists list their sound and lighting requirements — had been fully built but was unreachable anywhere in the app. Now accessible from the artist profile. Followed by a feature-by-feature review confirming everything we've built is genuinely reachable by a real user. Found a few more disconnected pieces, reconnected them all, and put a permanent rule in place so this can't quietly happen again.

log.title: Dark theme + per-role welcome testing in progress
log.detail: Cleared all remaining build warnings and set the app icon up properly. Working on restoring the dark visual theme — a recent change accidentally switched the app to a hard-to-read light look — and adding a quick way to test the full welcome experience for each of the five account types. Both in progress.

log.title: Restaurant brand applied to the template
log.detail: Started from a web template and transformed it into Number One Restaurant: replaced all placeholder text with the real name, tagline ('Shawarma & Falafel. Wiesbaden-Mitte.'), and address throughout. Set the colour scheme to deep black with amber and gold accents to match the restaurant's look and feel. The browser tab title and page identity are now all correct.

log.title: Full menu, prices + real photos added
log.detail: Built out the complete menu across 5 categories: Hähnchen-Shawarma (6 items), Fleisch-Shawarma (6 items including ½ kg and 1 kg sharing platters), Falafel & Mezze (9 items), the 3 signature hero dishes, and Drinks (5 items). Swapped in the restaurant's real food photography. Updated the phone number, opening hours (Mon–Thu + Sun until 23:00, Fri–Sat until midnight), and the Google rating (4.8★, 81 reviews).

log.title: Legal audit done — 5 GDPR problems found
log.detail: Before going live, ran a full scan of the site for legal and privacy issues. Found five things that had to be fixed: Google Maps was loading automatically and sending visitor data to Google without consent (a GDPR violation); the Impressum was missing (required by German law §5 DDG); the privacy policy was missing; the contact email was still a placeholder; and the owner name and tax number fields were blank.

log.title: Impressum, privacy policy + GDPR fixes done
log.detail: Added the Impressum (the legal disclosure page German law requires for any business website) and a full GDPR-compliant privacy policy. Fixed Google Maps so it only loads when the customer actively clicks 'KARTE LADEN' — Google never connects automatically. Updated the contact email (n1rw@wiesbaden.de) across every part of the site. Both legal documents open cleanly from the footer. Site is now legal to publish.

log.title: Site went live for the first time
log.detail: Built the final production version and deployed it to Vercel. Number One Restaurant now has a live public website — number-one-restaurant.vercel.app — for the first time.

log.title: Fully mobile + smooth animations throughout
log.detail: Full pass to make the site look professional on every screen size — the layout adapts from 3-column desktop down to single-column phone. Added: smooth entrance animations when the page loads; scroll-reveal for every section; staggered card pop-in; count-up numbers in the stats strip; a sticky frosted-glass navigation bar; a continuously scrolling amber info ticker; hover effects; and a pulsing 'jetzt offen' badge. All animations turn off automatically if the visitor's device has reduce-motion on.

log.title: German, English + Arabic (right-to-left) added
log.detail: Added a language switcher (DE · EN · عر) — every piece of text on the site is now in all three languages: navigation, menu items, descriptions, opening hours, address, and footer. When Arabic is selected, the entire page flips to right-to-left layout including the navigation and hero. Arabic uses the device's built-in system font so no outside connection is made — GDPR stays intact. The legal pages (Impressum, Datenschutz) remain in German only, as required by law. Final production build deployed.

log.title: Data-handling contract with Hetzner signed
log.detail: EU privacy law (GDPR) requires a signed contract with every company that stores your customers' data. We now have this contract (called an AVV) on file with Hetzner, our server provider. Hetzner is legally bound to follow EU privacy rules for the data stored on their servers in Falkenstein, Germany. Without this, we technically couldn't legally store customer or staff information on those servers.

log.title: TÜV security audit filed; legal status confirmed
log.detail: Filed a copy of Hetzner's latest independent security audit (carried out by TÜV Rheinland) — useful proof when a venue's accountant or a future investor asks whether our hosting is actually secure. Also clarified that since ThePuffer isn't yet a registered business, all contracts are correctly signed under Ali Hassan personally. Noted: register a Gewerbe at the Wiesbaden Gewerbeamt before invoicing a second venue or taking referral commissions.

log.title: EU-only storage area created for staff documents
log.detail: Set up a brand-new storage area at Cloudflare that is legally pinned to the European Union — data stored here can physically never leave EU borders. This is where all employment contracts, ID document scans, tax certificates, and other sensitive staff paperwork will now live. Kept separate from where we store things like product photos or app icons (those can sit anywhere).

log.title: EU storage wired into the backend
log.detail: Connected the new EU storage into the server's configuration so the app knows how to talk to it. There was a brief 90-second hiccup during the switchover — a temporary configuration drift that briefly hid some staff-onboarding code — caught and recovered without anyone noticing. Production stable; the lesson was documented so it won't happen again.

log.title: Staff documents now automatically go to EU storage
log.detail: Wrote, reviewed, and deployed the code change that makes every uploaded staff document (employment contract, ID scan, etc.) automatically land in the GDPR-protected EU storage. The system fails loudly if the EU storage is ever misconfigured — it will never silently fall back to a non-EU location by accident.

log.title: Full pipeline tested on real production servers
log.detail: Created a test staff member through the iOS app, uploaded a test document, and verified the whole chain: sensitive fields (IBAN, tax ID, social security number) are properly encrypted so even database admins can't read them; managers see masked values like DE89•••3000 not the raw IBAN; the document landed in EU storage, not the old one; and the delete function actually deletes everything, as EU privacy law requires. Test data was then cleanly purged. The full pipeline is now proven on real production traffic, not just in theory.

log.title: Document scan flow built in the iOS app
log.detail: Built the full Scannen (scan-to-hire) flow in the app: manager opens the camera or picks a photo, the app compresses it, sends it to the AI reader, shows a live 'reading...' countdown, and when the AI returns the results they land directly in the same editable review screen used by the Import tier. A real bug was caught during testing — the photo was being sent under the wrong label — found and fixed on the spot.

log.title: Full scan-to-hire verified on the test venue
log.detail: Ran the complete end-to-end journey on the SANDBOX test venue: photograph a payroll document → AI reads it → 12 fields extracted → manager reviews and saves → staff member created. Verified that sensitive fields (IBAN, tax ID) are masked in the manager view and that the document image is never stored anywhere. Test data was then cleanly purged from the system.

log.title: 14 staff roles now work correctly
log.detail: The database was silently rejecting common hospitality job titles — bartender, cook, server, host, busser, barback, security — even though the app offered them. All 14 roles (including manager and shift lead) are now accepted, with German error messages when something goes wrong and proper permission levels so a bartender can't access manager-only features.

log.title: Staff import screen redesigned
log.detail: The Import screen (where managers paste a list of staff from a spreadsheet) was rebuilt from scratch: each person now has their own roomy editable card instead of a dense row. Managers can select multiple people at once and change a setting for all of them in one go (e.g. 'set contract type for everyone'), edit any field inline, and sensitive details like IBAN show a locked symbol with a tap-to-reveal sheet. Live validation flags mistakes as you type.

log.title: AI document reader set up on Mac Studio
log.detail: Set up a local AI model (Gemma 4, running on the Mac Studio at home) that can read German payroll documents and extract the key fields — Steuer-ID, IBAN, social security number, name, address — as structured data. It's only accessible inside our private network (not the internet), so document images never leave our hands. Tested against a synthetic payroll form: all 12 fields extracted correctly, including exact IBAN and Steuer-ID digits.

log.title: Privacy assessment written for document scanning
log.detail: Wrote the formal privacy impact assessment (DPIA) required by EU law before we can scan real ID documents and payroll forms. It covers what data is processed, why, the risks, and the protections in place. Key finding: because the AI runs on our own Mac Studio rather than a cloud service, no ID document data ever leaves our control — which makes the compliance picture significantly simpler. Document is bilingual (German primary for the privacy authority, English working draft), ready for DPO sign-off.

log.title: Real-photo test done; faster AI model being evaluated
log.detail: Tested the scanner with a real phone-camera photo of a document (not the clean digital test used earlier). Found that the larger AI model takes longer than the timeout allows on real, imperfect photos — not because of image size, but because of the model's processing time. A smaller, faster model (about 5× quicker) is being evaluated as the solution. Download in progress; results expected shortly.

log.title: Faster document reader is live — under 6 seconds a photo
log.detail: Yesterday's open question is resolved: the smaller, quicker AI reader is now running and reading real phone-camera photos of forms in under 6 seconds each — roughly 5 to 50 times faster than before, depending on how dense the form is. Real, imperfect photos no longer time out the way the larger model did.

log.title: Onboard up to 30 new staff from photos in one sitting
log.detail: Patrick can now hire new staff by photographing their filled-in employment forms with his phone — up to 30 forms in a single session. The app reads each one, fills in the database fields, and shows everything in a review screen where he can check and correct before the staff records are created. For Wohnzimmer's pace (a handful of new hires a quarter) this turns half a day of typing into about a 15-minute session.

log.title: Which forms read cleanly — and which still need typing
log.detail: Honest status on form coverage: the common BDA, AOK and simple staff questionnaires read at 80–100% accuracy — names, dates of birth, tax IDs, phone numbers and emails come out reliably. The dense DATEV payroll form is the exception: names and tax IDs read fine, but Tax Class, Religion and Health Insurance don't reliably extract from its tight multi-column layout, so those are still filled in by hand. Hand-written forms aren't tested yet. Where the reader is unsure it writes 'empty' rather than guessing — a wrong value never slips in silently.

log.title: Scanner now survives the Mac sleeping or restarting
log.detail: The AI reader running on the in-office Mac used to quietly stop working after the machine went to sleep. It's now supervised — it restarts itself automatically after reboots and idle periods, and a second machine stands by as backup if the main one ever fails. No more silent outages.

log.title: Confidently-wrong bank & tax numbers made impossible
log.detail: Added a safety check that runs on every read: an IBAN or tax ID that doesn't pass its proper format check can no longer be saved as if it were correct — it's flagged as empty for the manager to fill in instead. This makes the worst kind of error — a wrong-but-plausible bank number that looks right — structurally impossible. Sensitive fields stay encrypted on the device and masked until tapped to reveal.

log.title: Privacy & compliance re-checked before go-live
log.detail: Walked the AVV-GDPR onboarding checklist again at each stage of the new flow — no regressions, and because the whole pipeline stays on hardware we control in the office, no ID-document data is ever sent to a third party. One genuine backend improvement was spotted and written up with the exact fix, queued for the second-venue rollout (current users aren't affected). The privacy assessment (DPIA) just needs a small model-name update before any external review.

log.title: Checking one bank-number mismatch from testing
log.detail: During late-night testing one IBAN came back not matching what was on the form. Looking into whether it's just a display quirk in the review screen or a real reading/validation issue before this goes in front of staff. Also a small follow-up to test against the AOK form. Headline for the day: photo-based staff onboarding is working in the test venue — Patrick can use it Monday, and multi-venue rollout becomes a real conversation.

log.title: Scannen accuracy blocked — daemon email validator
log.detail: Live app-service retest (SANDBOX) on real DATEV Personalfragebogen via api.thebarapp.de: 1/12 fields clean. email field corrupted with raw transcription tail (...Stand 08/2012"}) reproducible at both 1448x2048 and 2481x3509; page-2 502 at hi-res. env dump confirms relay -> :8044 GLM-OCR v0.4 (NOT Gemma :8043, NOT a deploy gap). Studio agent: v0.4 email-validator gap. iOS 2048 clamp verified correct/unified (no fix needed). PR #17 stays draft until daemon email-validator fix + retest passes.

log.title: Booking now works start to finish
log.detail: For the first time ever, a booking goes all the way through — from request, to confirmed, to done — and the invoice is created automatically. This was the single biggest thing that had never worked. The cause turned out to be a hidden database fault; it's now fixed and protected with a test so it can't quietly break again.

log.title: Real photos replace the placeholders
log.detail: The app now shows 60 real, made-for-us images for the artists and venues instead of stock photos. Besides looking far better, this removes a legal risk that came with using people's pictures without permission.

log.title: App running on a real iPhone
log.detail: Bloghead was installed and opened on an actual iPhone for the first time, connected to the live server — the animated intro, login, and real artist faces all working in hand. Until now it had only ever run on the computer.

log.title: Sign in with Google and Apple works
log.detail: Both 'Sign in with Google' and 'Sign in with Apple' were proven working on the live server — Apple for the very first time. Real accounts were created successfully through both.

log.title: The discovery feed is full of events
log.detail: The main feed used to be empty. It now shows 12 real upcoming events across Wiesbaden, Mainz and Frankfurt, sorted by how far away they are — so anyone opening the app sees something live and local right away.

log.title: Server now backs itself up every night
log.detail: Bloghead had no automatic backups — if the server died, recent work was gone. It now backs up nightly (kept for weeks), and a watchdog automatically restarts the app if it ever freezes, with an alert sent to the phone.

log.title: Payments — connecting Stripe
log.detail: Test payment keys are in hand and the payment system is being wired up so artists can actually get paid (with our 8% fee). It isn't live yet — this is the main thing standing between Bloghead and a working product.

log.title: A clear plan for the whole product
log.detail: Put the full vision through an expert review and locked a build order: first a lawful, polished shift-loop, then the bigger features later. Nothing was cut — just sequenced — with the legal lines drawn up front.

log.title: The gig loop works end to end
log.detail: Proved the heart of the product — a worker finds a shift, applies, gets accepted, and the job gets done — working all the way through on both the phone app and the venue dashboard, with a realistic test set (50 workers, 10 venues).

log.title: Fixed five important safety issues
log.detail: Closed five issues found in review — including making sure a worker can never open venue-only screens, and that a shift can't be accidentally filled twice.

log.title: Photos and chat made reliable
log.detail: Worker profile photos now upload properly, and the in-app chat reconnects reliably and shows your own messages correctly.

log.title: Right distances everywhere, not just Frankfurt
log.detail: The app had been assuming everyone was in Frankfurt, so shift distances were wrong for workers elsewhere. It now uses each worker's real city (e.g. Wiesbaden), so distances are correct across the region.

log.title: Running on a real iPhone
log.detail: Installed and opened on a real iPhone for the first time, connected to a live backend.

log.title: Three phone-only bugs found and fixed
log.detail: Testing on the real phone surfaced three issues — the keyboard hiding the chat 'send' button, an application that sent silently with no confirmation, and rows that weren't tappable. All three are fixed; the keyboard one needs one more check on a real keyboard before it's locked in.

log.title: Server prepared and everything backed up
log.detail: Set up everything the app needs to run on our server and pushed all the work to safe online storage, so nothing is stuck on one computer. The server isn't switched on yet — that waits on the website address and legal sign-off.

log.title: Held back the messaging feature on purpose
log.detail: Planned a richer messaging feature (templates and attachments) but deliberately put it on hold: it would add an outside AI service and make the legal approval bigger, right when legal is already the main thing holding up launch.

log.title: Waiting on legal sign-off and a domain to launch
log.detail: The code is nearly there, but launching for real is waiting on things outside coding: a lawyer's written OK, signed data-handling agreements with our service providers, and the website address plus its security certificate. The server is ready to switch on the moment those clear.

log.title: Closed a privacy gap between venues
log.detail: Found and fixed a serious issue where one venue could see another venue's reservations, regulars and assistant data. Fixed it, cleaned up the affected records, deployed to the live server, and proved each venue now only sees its own.

log.title: The assistant can now do things, not just chat
log.detail: The in-app assistant (Wozi) can now carry out real actions from a message — like reporting someone sick or offering a shift — and always asks you to confirm first, so nothing happens by accident.

log.title: New daily cash register (Tageskasse) — 'the bank'
log.detail: Built a daily till module: count the drawer at close and see the day's real profit. Built in a safe sandbox first so it could never touch live data by accident, then shipped to the live server switched off — ready to turn on for Das Wohnzimmer whenever you choose.

log.title: Daily till improved: other costs + polish
log.detail: Added 'other costs' (things paid out of the till or someone's own pocket) and polished the screens after a live demo. A test day came out to a clean profit of 1.541,80 €.

log.title: Built the digital menu module (Speisekarten)
log.detail: Venues can now build and edit their own menu in the dashboard, and it gets a clean public web page with its own link and a QR code — three polished design themes, allergen info, and proper German prices.

log.title: Make a menu from a photo, file, or your voice
log.detail: Added a way to fill a menu automatically — upload a photo or file of an existing menu, paste a link, or just speak it — and it drafts the items for you to review. For now this runs on test venues only, while we clear the data-protection steps before real venues use it.

log.title: Public menu page built for search & sharing
log.detail: Built the public menu website (menu.thebarapp.de) — fast, mobile-first and search-engine-friendly, with an embed option and print-to-PDF.

log.title: Privacy-safe staff avatars
log.detail: Designed simple drawn avatars for staff — not photos and not AI faces — so the schedule and feed feel personal without ever storing anyone's picture. Built; waiting on a final check on a real phone.

log.title: Fixed the shift-offer phone notification
log.detail: Fixed an issue where the 'a shift was offered to you' phone notification was being silently dropped. Fixed; needs one check on a real phone to confirm tap-through and accept/decline.

log.title: Waiting on Apple, the tax advisor & a phone check
log.detail: The app is feature-complete and healthy. The last steps to the public beta are outside coding: Apple's review of the latest build, the tax advisor's confirmed VAT rates (to switch the till from gross to net), and two quick checks on a real phone.

log.title: User photos & audio now survive restarts
log.detail: Profile pictures, cover images and audio clips were being wiped every time the server was updated, because they were stored in a temporary spot with no safe home. They now live in a permanent, protected location that survives restarts. Also added a fair-use limit (30 uploads per hour per person) so no one can flood the storage, and prepared a one-switch move to cloud storage (Cloudflare) for when that account is turned on. All 1010 automated checks pass.

log.title: Build and edit menus on the iPhone
log.detail: The whole menu editor now works on the iPhone, not just the dashboard — add cards, categories and dishes, choose a design, and import a menu by photo or voice, all from the phone.

log.title: Menu dishes show real food photos
log.detail: Menu items can now show professional food photos — uploaded or generated automatically — kept on our own European servers. The public menu also comes in seven designs with custom colours and fonts to match each venue.

log.title: Menu polish — awaiting your phone sign-off
log.detail: Added smooth, premium animations throughout the menu screens (transitions, a live voice waveform, image fades). Built and on the phone — the last step is a quick feel-check on your iPhone.

log.title: Faster, steadier sign-in under load
log.detail: Signing in no longer slows the whole app down when several people log in at once, and when the server gets very busy it now backs off gracefully instead of throwing errors. Also fixed a hidden startup-crash risk in the server settings. Deployed to the live server and verified working (real sign-in went through end-to-end).

log.title: Payments are wired up (test mode)
log.detail: The payment system now works end-to-end in test mode — a booking can be paid with our 8% fee shown, using test cards (no real money yet). It clears the last big functional gap before real charges.

log.title: Fixed a friend's 9 bugs and the light theme
log.detail: Merged a batch fixing the nine issues a friend found while testing, plus a full light-theme cleanup and booking-form and date fixes.

log.title: Tested for a crowd, added downtime alerts
log.detail: Load-tested the app for 50–100 people at once (reads held up with zero errors), and added a monitor that alerts us within minutes if the app ever goes down.

log.title: First TestFlight build uploaded
log.detail: The first TestFlight build is uploaded and processing in Apple's App Store Connect. It's internal testing, so no Apple review is needed — once it finishes processing, a friend can install it on their iPhone.

log.title: Now in demo testing at Das Wohnzimmer
log.detail: TheBarApp is being tried out as a demo at Das Wohnzimmer to gather feedback — it isn't in daily production use there yet. Going live for real is the next milestone.

log.title: Whole app checked, 124 fixes found
log.detail: Built an automated walkthrough that opens every screen of the app — artist side, venue side and fan side, in both light and dark mode — takes a picture of each, then reviewed all 76. Found 124 things to improve. The biggest by far: lots of the app still shows English text even though it should be German, plus several screens are hard to read in light mode. Also set up a repeatable test so we can re-check the whole app anytime in minutes. A prioritized fix list is ready.

log.title: Bloghead now has a web version
log.detail: Built a full browser version of the Bloghead app overnight — same look, same photos, same data as the phone app. People can sign in, browse artists and venues, send a booking request through the step-by-step flow (with the 8% fee shown), sign the contract, chat in real time, and manage their profile. A full booking was run from request all the way to a finished invoice to prove it works. It's all tested with screenshots and saved as a draft for review — nothing is live yet. Still needs payment keys and a Google/Apple web login before launch.

log.title: Filmed the full booking deal, both sides
log.detail: Recorded a screen-capture walkthrough of the concert-booking flow inside the iPhone app, switching between the event organiser and the artist accounts. It shows the finished deal from both sides — the signed contract lifecycle (requested → accepted → contract → confirmed → completed) and the PAID invoice (Rechnung 2026-001, 1.800,00 €). Along the way fixed two app bugs uncovered by the recording: the accounting screen crashed on the invoice list, and the sign-in could load the wrong saved account.

log.title: Whole hiring journey works end-to-end
log.detail: Walked and recorded the full flow on the workforce app: a venue posts a shift → it shows up for a nearby worker → the worker applies → the venue accepts (a chat opens) → the venue marks the shift complete. All real, captured as one video. Also smoothed a few rough spots from the app walkthrough (a stuck "skills" section, a full shift still labelled "open", a report button that looked like a plain link) — ready for your review, not yet live. One gap found: there's no "congratulations" screen when a worker finishes their first shift — that moment passes silently.

log.title: All three booking flows proven, with videos
log.detail: Recorded full demo videos of all three ways a booking happens on Bloghead — an artist offering a venue, an organiser booking an artist, and a fan booking an artist for a private party. Each runs the whole way through: request, accept, contract, both signatures, the event finishing, the invoice, and getting paid. Swapped the placeholder cartoon avatars for real photos. Also found and fixed a bug that was stopping contract signing from working inside the app.

log.title: Card payments fixed and live
log.detail: Card payments now work end-to-end. The card is only reserved when the customer pays, and the money is taken only after BOTH sides sign the contract — so no one is charged before the deal is sealed. Fixed the bug that stopped payments from starting, deployed to the live server (test mode), and verified it there. The 8% platform fee is applied correctly. The web version's checkout was matched to the same rules and proven locally. (Bank-transfer/SEPA and the public website launch are intentionally left for later.)

log.title: Booking deal works inside the app
log.detail: Before, the booking lifecycle only worked behind the scenes — in the actual app the "Generate contract" button did nothing and there was no working payment step. Now every step works by tapping the real app: for all three deal types (artist↔venue, organiser↔artist, fan↔artist) the deal goes request → contract → both sign with a code → pay by card → done, with the invoice marked paid. Filmed end-to-end on a test phone. On a branch, tested only, not yet live.

log.title: Menu assistant now updates the menu live
log.detail: Owners can type a menu change in plain language in the dashboard's AI assistant — e.g. a new price — review it, and confirm. The change is now applied to the live menu immediately (before, confirming only marked the request without changing anything). Proven end-to-end on a test venue: a dish price went 10,50 € → 12,00 € and back. The dashboard fix is live now; the matching change for the phone app is prepared and will ship with the next app update.

log.title: Card payment screen works in the app
log.detail: The card-payment screen (Apple's secure card sheet) now actually opens and works inside the iPhone app: you enter the card, it gets authorised, and the money is only taken after both sides sign the contract — proven on a test phone and screen-recorded (test mode, nothing charged for real). I also set up three test accounts (a dev artist, venue and booker) so the whole booking can be run end-to-end on your own phone, with the sign-in codes coming to your email. Next: a new test build for you to try it, then your on-device check.

log.title: Workers get a celebration after each shift
log.detail: Added a "well done" moment for workers when they finish shifts — first shift, then at 5, 10, 25 and 50. Proven on a real run: a venue posts a job, the worker applies, gets accepted, both chat, the venue marks it complete, and the celebration fires. Also tidied everything into one clean, up-to-date version of the app, and fixed two display glitches: a profile screen showing internal labels, and a message template that left "…" blanks in messages to venues.

log.title: Deal, signing and payment work together
log.detail: All three booking types (artist↔venue, organiser→artist, fan→artist) now run the FULL deal inside the app on one build: send request → generate contract → both sides sign with a code → card is really charged → invoice created. Charges use the proper "hold now, take the money once both have signed" model, verified with real test-card payments and filmed for each flow. Sits on a review branch (draft) — not live yet; one payment-order safeguard still to add before go-live.

log.title: Read the contract before signing it
log.detail: The app now shows the actual contract document. After a contract is created it opens automatically so you can read the full terms — who, fee, date, cancellation — as a proper PDF. You must see it before the signing code step, and once both sides have signed, the signed contract (with both signatures and timestamps) stays viewable and shareable for both the artist and the organiser. Proven in the running app with screen recordings.

headlines: Bloghead's booking flow now runs end-to-end for the first time — request, to confirmed, to invoice, automatically.
Bloghead is running on a real iPhone, pointed at the live server — animated intro, login and real photos all working.
Sign in with Google and Apple are both proven on the live server — Apple for the very first time.
The discovery feed is live: 12 real upcoming events across Wiesbaden, Mainz and Frankfurt.
Bloghead now backs itself up every night, with a watchdog that auto-restarts it if it ever freezes.
Next up for Bloghead: wiring Stripe so artists actually get paid.
